papers.title: Centering Community-Rooted Actions of Hope: Beyond Knowledge Monoculture
papers.authors: Miwa Aoki Takeuchi, Deborah Dutta, Fernanda Coelho Liberali, Tyrell Anderson, Racquel Banazsak, Michael Bakal, Voces y Manos, Michael Cole, Moises Esteban-Guitart, Institut de Recerca Educativa, Lisa Ghost, Kris Gutiérrez, Shakhnoza Kayumova, the Un ited States, Erma Mujic, Preeti Patil, Founder of Urban Leaves, Antti Rajala, Université de Neuchâtel, George Spears, Darci Ann Sigana
papers.abstract: Our sym posium is a confluence of researchers/pedagogues/designers /practitioners who embrace porousness of these identity categories, toward collectively questioning and challenging knowledge and environmental monoculture (Shiva, 1993). We recognize the resurgence of endangered ways of knowing and ways of living as a necessary intervention to environmental destruction and coloniality. While facing the overwhelming devastation of environmental degradation and repercussions from globalization and col onialism, we refuse to cede with ontological negation (Bang, 2020). Instead, we together seek to ground ourselves in community-rooted praxis and pedagogy of hope ( Freire, 1992; Gutiérrez, 2016). We collectively present locally and globally relevant socio- environmental issues that arose from communities beyond academic siloes. Together, we highlight community-based actions of hope representing diverse geographical localities and histories. Collectively, we gesture toward knowledge polyculture that is life affirming and orients us toward plural alternative visions of multi-species flourishing. Framing our dialogue: Stewarding plural multi-species flourishing In problematizing knowledge production systems that force Indigenous activists and their communities to talk back to and talk up to power, Smith (2012) argued ethics and integrity in telling the story right and well. This provocation touches upon ethics and values embedded in subject-subject relations or relationships between social actors in research, but also encompasses into subject-object relations that need to be fundamentally scrutinized in participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). Without critical examination on “what forms of knowledge are generated, how, why, where, and by whom” (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016, p. 174), researchers in the learning sciences might risk perpetuating normative hierarchy of power. Pointing out the violence embedded in globalized, hegemonic forms of knowledge acquisition, Visvanathan (2009) calls for cognitive justice in recognizing that knowledges go beyond purely epistemic but are embedded in ecologies, life-worlds, cosmologies and livelihoods. Taking seriously the diverse ways of knowing, in their vital, dialogic form (as opposed to curated and extractive abstractions) engenders democratic and equitable forms of inquiry. Movements toward cognitive justice share visions for epistemic justice that seek to redress marginalization and oppression through testimonial credibility, access to information, and the availability of proper representation (Fricker, 2013; Penuel & Watkins, 2019). Yet, gesturing toward cognitive justice has a distinct orientation to interrogating the repercussions of globalization, histories of colonization, and environmental destruction, which resulted from and resulted in endangering the lived knowledge of the most vulnerable, being entangled with ecology and plural ways to live. In this context, our symposium gathers  researchers/pedagogues/activists/designers who share concerns for locally and globally relevant socio-environmental justice issues, while representing diversity in geographical, geopolitical locality and histories. We all take the question of telling the story right and well seriously, and engage 2318 in constant reflection on ethics, responsibility, and morals in research-based storytelling toward what Visvanathan (2009) envisioned as cognitive justice. We share visions for social design experiments rooted in “a  place of hope and possibility, stemming out of the material reality that there are many groups of people who have been, an d continue to be, oppressed as a result of systemic injustice” (Gutiérrez et al., 2020, p. 332). We contemplate on the forms of knowledge creation that could mediate the process of participants becoming designers of their own futures, especially in the context of socio -environmental justice issues at stake. While facing the overwhelming devastation of environmental degradation and the spread of “seeds that have been modified through settler - colonialism,” we refuse “the ceding of ontological ground to negations” (Bang, 2020, p. 438). Instead, we together seek to ground our work in the “grammar of hope, possibility, and resilience” (Gutiérrez, 2016, p. 188). We embrace our collective hope with decolonial love (Betasamosake Simpson, 2013)— “ love that resists the nature- culture or nature-society divide, love to know our responsibilities and enact them in ways that give back, and love that does not neglect historical oppression and violence yet carries us through” ( Takeuchi & Marin, 2022, p.1). Countering epistemic hegemony entails critically questioning the dominant paradigms of reason, growth and development that have come to define the standards and modes of learning and living. The closely coupled system of capitalistic exploitation and reductive, disembodied techno-scientific rationality has tried to build socio- cultural narratives that value parameters such as profit, scale, uniformity and efficiency over ideas of reciprocity, contextual appropriateness, relationality and interdependence (Date et al., 2021). Rooted in pioneering environmental activism work in India, Vandana Shiva (1993) problematized “monocultures of the mind,” the ways in which modern agri-science with its focus on narrow conceptions of yields of a few staple grains erased and delegitimised Indigenous knowledge systems based on soil ecology, plant health, pest -predator relationships and seed sovereignty. Shiva (1993) has warned  that monocultures of the mind would result in environmental degradation, depleted biodiversity, impoverished diets and food apartheid, and loss of livelihoods, all of which affect the most vulnerable in globalized systems of power. The modern myth of productivity to stall scarcity is built on assumptions of competition and control. In Epistemologies of the South, Boaventura de Sousa Santos (2015) refers to such systems of thought as lazy reasoning, explaining that deterministic, dualistic, the supposed infallibility of progress -based arguments only serves to highlight the arrogance and ultimate ignorance underlying the dominant narrative. Moving away from these self-destructive and life -impoverishing socio-technical monocultures requires nurturing diverse ecologies of thought and mediums of knowledge  beyond coloniality (de Sousa Santos, 2015; Mignolo, 2007). Bringing to fore the  marginalized counterfactual knowledges and lived experiences demands imagination and courage to explore the range of possibilities existing in community-oriented praxis of resistance and hope (Freire, 1992). Our symposium is an invitation to broaden these possibilities  and steward the ecosystems that allow for multiple alternative visions of multi- species flourishing and well -being to manifest. Toward this, we seek reflections from people working deeply in communit ies, are mindful of coloniality and cultivating decolonial present/future, and have been taking community-rooted actions aligned with cognitive justice. Many of us in this symposium spend hours grounding ourselves in community, engage in dialogues with multiple stakeholders, and create mediums of communication beyond conventional academic publications. Our symposium brings together heterogeneous voices of an intergenerational group of scholars and community-based or school -based practitioners. Our symposium is an orchestration of  voices rooted in community and highlighting diversity in geographical, geopolitical localities and histories. With curated hybrid engagement spaces, we invite voices from teachers, community workers, families , and researchers. Each group of presenters in this symposium will share their work using the following guiding questions: 1) What is the context in which you are working? 2) In what ways, your work disrupts a particular monoculture of knowledge system? In other words, what issue prompted your specific research/educational engagement? 3) What forms of learning your work has tried to center and nurture? 4) How do you see your work contributing to community-rooted actions of hope? Situated in the urban context of India, Dutta, Patil , and Mukherjee together cultivate hope (Dutta & Hazra, 2023), for community-based environmental stewardship to rewrite the images of Mumbai as a metropolitan space for human -centered activities. Kayumova shares her longitudinal project that positions racia lized multilingual youth at the center of radical possibilities for reimagining social, cultural and environmental futures rooted in care, relationality, and interdependence —a pluriverse of STEM discipline (Kayumova & Dou, 2022). In the context of Indigenous -led public schools in Mní Sóta Makhóčhe and Storywalks (Marin & Bang, 2018), Meixi, Banazsak, Spears, Sigana, Ghost, Anderson, and Mujic together illuminate how the Land teaches us about how we live relationally (Meixi & Nzinga, 2024; Wildcat, 2013 ). Drawing from their community -engaged co- design efforts in the Maya-Achí community, Bakal and Gutiérrez leverage a telos of Buen Vivir (Bakal & Reyes, 2023) as a key principle for social design-based experiment (Gutiérrez et al., 2020) toward a utopian future. From 2319 the praxis of utopian methodologies ( Rajala, Cole, & Esteban -Guitart, 2023) and highlighting non- linearity and heterochronicity, Rajala, Cole, and Esteban-Guitart illustrate tangible utopias in rural and urban schools in Finland through sustainable futures projects enacted by teachers, and in collaboration with the municipal government . Following co-chair’s framing (8 minutes), each group will present their work in 12 minutes each (a total of 60 minutes), followed by synthesizing commentary from our discussant and conversations with the audiences. Liberali’s commentary as a discussant draws from her longitudinal praxis rooted in critical, counter-colonial, and history-making imaginaries. Liberali’s theoretical works are rooted in her designed practices and also lived experiences situated in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo  (Liberali, 2019) , re flecting languages, diversities, and education to redress socio-environmental and socio-economical injustices. Her remarks will deepen our collective visions for fostering alternative knowledge systems that are not hegemonic and colonial. Our hybrid symposium will create a space that hosts each team’s stories and related academic and public works, which can be a resource for sustained discussion. Collectively, our symposium intends to nurture sustained dialogues including collective sharing of unfinished thoughts and questions, with the Learning Sciences community. Cultivating hope: Reflections on community urban gardening experiences in India to reimagine human-nature relationships in cities Deborah Dutta, Preeti Patil, Samira Mukherjee Studies estimate nearly 60 percent of the population will be living  in urban areas by 2050 (Cohen, 2006). The growth of cities is especially noticeable in the Global South, with an aggressive expansion of urban areas. The ‘development’ trajectories employed in  the creation of urban spaces largely borrow from the Global North and capital-intensive, industrial narratives, thus relying on pipeline models of resource extraction (Shiva, 1993). The design of cities has been critiqued by practitioners and scholars for creating a “ metabolic rift” as part of its exploitative processes of sustaining itself at the expense of other ecosystems (Dutta, 2024). As myriad forms of socio-ecological crises proliferate, with cities being responsible for a significant amount of carbon emissions, waste production and material consumption),  there is an urgent need to reimagine our relationship, roles, and place in cities. The issue is of special significance to the field of learning sciences, given the increasing scholarship on embodied and emplaced dimensions of learning, which also form the basis for socio-political action (Takeuchi & Marin, 2022). Critical attention to the geographical and socio-ecological infrastructure of urban spaces thus has implications for ways in which the situated, embodied and cultural aspects of learning and living are envisioned. In our projects, we focused on urban food systems as a domain of practice and reflection. The socio -economic arrangements and often opaque supply chains in cities are entangled with questions of food security and nutrition in fundamental ways. As Frazier (2018) explains, “Food is a productive site for exploring the intimate intersection of bodies and cities. This is in part due to the inextricable relationship between food, the body, and place. As scholars have long identified, food is a symbolic and material force that transcends and delimits particular places and communities” (p.12). Linking the act of consuming food to the conditions under which food is grown and brought to our plates requires an empathetic, systemic way of thinking about the human –nature relationship. The context and methodology Our projects explored community-based stewardship or “civic ecology” practices (Krasny & Tidball, 2012) based on the principle of humans nested within larger socio-ecological systems and being able to impact the systems in positive ways through feedback and virtuous cycles of empowerment. Drawing on Social Design- Experiments approach (Gutiérrez, 2016), our efforts call for attention to the dynamic nature of cultural interactions with food, soil, and plants and how these mediate transformative trajectories for individuals and communities. The approach focuses on resilience stemming from emergent, systemic changes within the community. Our collective experiences of volunteering at an urban community garden, facilitating a school-terrace garden and collaborating with community partners served to highlight the evolving knowledge and perspectives that grew along with the spaces, as they transformed into alternate visions of cityscapes ranging from local campaigns to save native seeds, petition against GMO crops, and a renewed interest in traditional farming practices adapted for urban spaces. Findings and contributions Together, these initiatives illustrate that i) feedback and competency arising from sustained interaction with artefacts in community -based practices motivate individual sphere of actions, which can then extend into the wider community, ii) ecological perspectives are embedded in 'performative' substances such as compost, native seeds, manure etc as interacting with these entities allowed growers to understand the embedded views towards nature in an embodied (i.e. non- descriptive) way, while also recreating  in an urban setting agricultural practices 2320 that are rapidly disappearing from India’s villages.  iii) embodied encounters are central to developing care-based relationships with the environment, and iv) shared- practices support extending ecological actions to the wider community. Many participants reported developing pro- environmental values such as frugality, re -usability and promoting biodiversity, which emerged through sustained participation in group activities that embed these principles. This indicates that ecological practices such as community farming are a way to help implicitly develop an alternative value system towards the environment, and generate the rich, moral imagination necessary to think and act in ways to promote multispecies flourishing (as seen in our illustrated narratives, Dutta & Hazra, 2023). Given the atrophied and opaque nature of socio -ecological relationships in cities, facilitating such rich experiences, and understanding the challenges of  acting upon them offer a promising trajectory for research in learning sciences. These initiatives also question the development narratives and urban architecture usually taken for granted in city planning by actively positioning alternate visions for just, sustainable futures. Stories and visions of hope: Visibilizing multilingual young people’s onto- epistemological brilliance in STEM education Shakhnoza Kayumova Despite reforms and interventions, racial and linguistic inequities persist within STEM education for youth from nondominant communities, reflecting entrenched deficit -based discourses and an ongoing framing of “lack” in students’ skills, identities, and engagement. This study contends that to disrupt these discourses, it is essential to interrogate the foundational logic of dominant epistemological and ontological (e.g., neutrality, objectivity, and universality) assumptions of disciplinary education. In t he U.S. public schools, emergent bilingual/multilingual youth tend to be entrenched with the deficit discourse that gets inscribed in tools of learning imbued with epistemic injustices (Harper & Kayumova, 2023) . The overwhelming emphasis is placed on academic language development, assuming that language is the primary mediator of learning, devoid of racial and colonial struggles (Takeuchi et al., 2022). As Escobar (2018) described, “[t]o think new thoughts, by implication, requires stepping out of the epist emic space of Western social theory and into the epistemic configurations associated with the multiple relation ontologies of worlds in struggle” (p. 68). The context and methodology The data for this study comes from a longitudinal research program aimed at understanding the intersection between language- based racialization and science identity development among multilingual youth from nondominant communities. Over six years, youth pa rticipated in a 2-week all-day summer program engaging in STEM projects tackling sustainability issues in their community. The overall goal of the program was to understand what it means to dismantle deficit-based discourses rooted in raciolinguistic ideologies by positioning multilingual youth in asset-based terms and subsequently equipping youth with tools to re-position themselves as cognitively advantaged. Within the program, we drew on theories of pluriverse and positioning to co-design asset- based learning spaces in which the students, teachers, and researchers were positioned as co -authors, co- researchers, and co-creators of knowledge. Given the longitudinal nature of the work, over the years we witnessed how local sustainability and environmental justice issues as a framework in the context of STEM allowed young people and teachers to explore the interconnectedness of inequities in disciplinary, social, and environmental spheres. Findings and contributions Our findings show that when youth’s home and community ways of being and knowing were centered as focal in disciplinary learning, their marginalized identities, as discussed by hooks (1991) and Wynter ( 1989), became integral to the radical possibilities  for reimagining social, cultural, and environmental futures based on care, relationality, and interdependence. In these spaces, as youth and educators engaged with issues like food justice, soil degradation, and environmental harms, their practice of relatio nality as an epistemic approach enabled them to “see, hear, and listen” to the living and more -than-living entities around them, grounding their disciplinary sensemaking in responsive, interconnected ways. Further examining the interconnected nature of these inequities, educators and youth began to explore how scientists and engineers are not merely documenting a world “out there” or designing detached solutions; rather, they are actively shaping reality through the models, definitions, and systems they cre ate. This awareness opened a space for reflecting on how the dehumanization experienced by multilingual youth within the culture of their schooling was connected to broader epistemic violence —where dominant assumptions of neutrality, objectivity, and unive rsality in disciplinary fields contribute to both the marginalization of human identities and the devaluation of nature (Kayumova & Dou, 2023). 2321 Youth, teachers and researchers came to see how the same epistemological and ontological frameworks that render certain forms of knowledge and experience invisible or invalid in their own lives also underpin a worldview that dehumanizes and exploits natural systems, framing both people and the environment as resources to be managed rather than as interconnected beings with intrinsic worth. Building on this critical lens, the youth developed innovative projects that embodied both disciplinary ingenuity and holistic worldviews. They created smart-sensing food conservation boxes and designed “living” smart homes that incorporated mushrooms as natural decomposers and filtration systems for water, all while exploring energy harvesting through fluid dynamics. We argue that deficit views of multilingual youth not only harm them by implying they must fragment their identities to engage in STEM but also alienate them “from the real socio -scientific challenges their communities face, failing to position them as essential contributors to urgently needed solutions” (Bang & Marin, 2015, p. 531). Through youth’s endeavors for environmental justices, they demonstrated how STEM practices could be reimagined to honor care, relationality and reciprocity reflecting a transformat ive ethic that not only challenged monoculture of dominant onto -epistemologies but also contributed to a collective hope for socially- environmentally just and thriving visions of living and futures. Land teaches us how we are related: Designing towards collective continuance through indigenous-led public schools Meixi, Racquel Banazsak, George Spears, Darci Ann Sigana, Lisa Ghost, Tyrell Anderson, Erma Mujic In a rapidly shifting and turbulent world, we have been deeply concerned with how schools might support a communities’ collective continuance—their collective capacities for a people to continue into the future (Whyte, 2017). We know that turbulent times are drastically uneven for Indigenous, Black, trans and queer, working class communities, and other people of color (Ladson -Billings, 2021) . Indigenous peoples have historically been through multiple pandemics —including the theft of land, boarding schools, and massive social and ecological destruction and upheaval —and therefore have millennia -old strategies for navigating the changes of the f uture (Meixi & Nzinga, 2024). Focusing on Storywalks as community members in the Franklin Avenue neighborhood, this paper explores Storywalks as a practice of reading, walking, and storying lands across families and educators (Marin & Bang, 2018). Given that a community's collective continuance is predicated on the moral relations and ethical commitments that members of a collective have to each other, we focus this paper on how storywalking revealed and renewed key relations embedded within Lands and the openings that these created for future-making together. The context and methodology The Storywalks featured here are hosted by families of Nawayee Center School, located in the historic Franklin Avenue neighborhood and American Indian Corridor in Minneapolis, Mní Sóta Makhóčhe (in Dakota, where the waters reflect the skies). We ask: How might centering families, lands and stories, reveal, enact, and renew community ethical expertise and relational commitments in Indigenous -led public school contexts? What might we learn from Indigenous educators and strategists who have been organizing and designing educational systems in spite of being occupied? Nawayee Center School is a contracted 7 th - 12th grade alternative school with a yearly enrollment of about 45 students. It is located in the heart of a diverse urban community in Minneapolis that is home to over 35,000 Native people), traditional and contemporary Dakota homelands that is also home to m any Ojibwe and Ho- Chunk people. The only remaining “survival school” (Davis, 2013) in the cities, Nawayee was born of vibrant intergenerational histories of almost 55 years of community- based activism and organizing since the late 1960s and was a particularly rich site for these walks together. Findings and contributions In our analysis, we draw from video data with students and community members as we moved around the lands and waterways in Minneapolis from September 2023—October 2024. Activities during this time included various guardian circle events, art workshops, and an Indigenous waterways camp. These events were designed and implemented by Nawayee Center School educators, community members and University researchers.  We particularly attended to critical historicity and future building through engagement with elders, exploring local Land and waterways, and learning Indigenous histories and practices (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) . One key finding is that Land teaches us how we are related. On one level, this meant that land and waterscapes were holders of intergenerational life at multiple timescales - cosmological, geologic, plant time, and in imagining futures. Secondly, plants - and milkweed in specific, connected us in trans -Indigenous relations. Learning the specific roles and responsibilities of milkweed supported understanding connections across 2322 geographies specifically across educators in Chiapas, Mexico and Minneapolis. Finally, walking Lands was helpful in considering how we are restor(y)ing place - at ecological, political, and social levels - and the role of Indigenous presence in this endeavor. We find that Storywalking foundationally reorients learning at school towards community relationships to place and the renewal of the ethical bonds and expertise that reside in beloved community spaces. It is important for us to note however, it is the  ongoing history of relations prior to walking together, the kinds of relationalities enacted on these walks, and the possibilities of such renewal in the future were core to designing for our collective continuances as Franklin Avenue community members. As living relations are continually in flux and motion, more intentionally attending to our daily rounds disrupted traditional methods of learning by engaging whole -bodied intelligences with lands and each other (Betasamosake Simpson, 2013). Storywalks as a relational practice took seriously the rich tapestry of intergenerational family life at school and positioned the  school as a place of cultivating community hope, a kind of design towards collective continuance in loved places. papers.abstract: As emerging digital technologies and AI reshape education, Computational Thinking (CT) skills such as abstraction, problem decomposition, and algorithm design are crucial for learners to navigate this landscape. This symposium brings together a set of diverse studies that highlight the relevance of CT  and problem -solving skills in the age of AI. The studies demonstrate how CT can be comprehensively addressed in learning sciences research at different educational levels from primary school to teacher education, in different learning designs spanning from individual programming tasks to collaborative activities, and through multimodal multichannel data. The discussion will focus on the relevance of CT as a core concept supporting learning with and about AI while preserving critical pedagogical values such as agency, creativity, and critical thinking with human-centered approaches. Overview of the symposium In today’s  educational landscapes driven by artificial intelligence (AI), our theoretical and empirical understanding of such transversal skills and competences as computational thinking (CT) and problem solving that are foundational for learners undergo significant transformation. CT is increasingly recognized as a specific form of problem solving that involves processes such as abstraction, decomposition, and algorithmic thinking. As digital technologies and AI tools reshape how we learn, teach, and design learning environments, there is a growing need to explore how these skills evolve in these contexts. Our symposium offers a timely and comprehensive exploration of CT and problem-solving skills in the age of AI, with a dual focus: (1) showcasing diverse theoretical and methodological approaches to investigating these skills in various educational settings, and (2) interrogating the role of these skills in AI -supported learning and teaching across different educational levels. CT refers to a competence that allows us  to solve complex problems  with a creative problem -solving approach relying on computational concepts and cognitive processes such as abstraction, problem decomposition, algorithm design, and debugging (Romero et al., 2017) . Rather than simply coding line by line , i t involves developing an approach to solve complex problems  by engaging in a reflective and creative analysis of the situation, its representation at the abstract and concrete levels, and the operationalization of a solution  that is produced with the help of metacognitive strategies  associated with CT , which can be applicable to different contexts and situations, not only in computer programming (Romero et al., 2024). While early research on CT predominantly emphasized individual learning outcomes —such as individual task behavior in programming environments (Guenaga et al., 2021) —and was often grounded in cognitivist perspectives (Agbo et al., 2021), recent studies have expanded this scope. Emerging work increasingly explores CT as a socially situated and collaborative process (e.g., Lai & Wong, 2022; Lee et al., 2019) , drawing on constructivist and/or experiential learning theories (Agbo et al., 2021). Consequently, there is an increasing interest in studying various aspects of human behavior involved in learning CT, such as participation, social interaction, and interest (Kafai et al., 2020)  as well as collaboration and regulation of learning processes (Emara et al., 2021). Despite this shift, there remains a need for more integrative studies that examine CT development in situ, capturing the interplay of individual, social, and technological dimensions. Addressing this, our symposium brings together studies that investigate CT across a range of educational contexts —from elementary classrooms to teacher education—and at different levels of analysis, i.e., from individual performance to group collaboration. By employing diverse methods, including multimodal multichannel data (e.g., log files, video, screen and audio recording), these studies contribute novel insights into the dynamic, contextual nature of CT. Collectively, they 2469 advance a more holistic understanding of CT as it unfolds in authentic, technology-rich learning environments— an essential step toward theorizing CT in the age of AI. Building on this broader view of CT as a dynamic, socially embedded, and context-sensitive competence, recent research has increasingly examined the evolving relationship between CT and AI. Studies have  not only suggested that CT and problem -solving skills positively impact AI literacy (Celik, 2023) , but also that the relationship is reciprocal—AI can in turn support the development and application of CT skills (Guggemos, 2024). However, as AI technologies become more deeply embedded in educational practices, they are reshaping core problem-solving CT processes such as  debugging (Sun et al., 2024a ). This transformation calls for deeper theoretical and empirical inquiry into how AI-driven learning environments differ from traditional approaches to CT instruction—not merely as tools but rather as co- agents in learning. Against this backdrop, our symposium’s second aim is to explore this evolving theme and its pedagogical implications. In particular, we emphasize the central role of teachers not only in integrating AI meaningfully into their classrooms (Celik, 2023; Luckin et al., 2016), but also in fostering learners’ critical engagement with computational systems. The presented studies shed light on how educators can leverage CT as a framework to both teach about AI  and teach with AI— highlighting human-centered pedagogical approaches that empower learners to navigate, critique, and co -create within increasingly algorithmic educational landscapes (Romero et al., 2024). To operationalize our two central aims , (1) understanding CT development across contexts  and (2) exploring its evolving conceptualization in AI-supported environments, we present five diverse yet conceptually connected studies. Together, they offer a rich set of methodological approaches and theoretical insights. papers.title: Authenticity and Entomology Knowledge in Science Classrooms
papers.authors: David Stroupe, Megan Walser, Peter White
papers.abstract: A long- standing goal of science education has been for students to engage in “authentic” science. This goal of authentic science has appeared in many policy documents, and most recently, in the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS, Achieve, 2013)  in the United States. Thirteen years after the release of NGSS, we still wonder about how to support students to engage in “authentic” science in classrooms.  Our presentation will examine relationships between authenticity, epistemic agency, and uncertainty, and equity. The presentations will approach the topic in two ways: expectations and norms for students, and the role of teachers. Students may be engaging in “authentic” science when they are exercising epistemic agency. We will conclude with questions for the field to consider. Purpose A long- standing goal of science education has been for students to engage in “authentic” science, which has appeared in many policy documents, and most recently, in the Next Generation Science Standards in the United States (NGSS, Achieve, 2013). Thirteen years after the release of NGSS, the field of science education still wonders how to support students’ engagement in “authentic” science. We propose that any discussion about “authentic” science must include: • Epistemic agency (the power and responsibility to shape knowledge production in a context, Stroupe, 2014) • Uncertainty (the inherent unpredictability that emerges from social interactions, Manz & Suárez, 2018) • Equity (disrupting power structures to create opportunities for justice, Burgess & Patterson Williams, 2022). In this session, we place epistemic agency, uncertainty, and equity in conversation with authenticity to advance a needed conversation for the field. Framing We propose that conversations about authenticity parallel issues of power. Authorities in classrooms, such as teachers and scientists, ask students to trust their expertise, yet people in positions of scientific power have sometimes caused lasting harm to people without power (see History of The National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition, 2020, & Jones, 1981). To address issues of power and authenticity, we report on the InsectLife project. InsectLife explores how elementary and middle school teachers partner with university- based entomologists to support students as to engage in authentic science and co- design moth research. We ask: • How do actors in InsectLife define authenticity and power in science classrooms ? • How do actors design and enact opportunities for students to engage in authentic science? We utilize Cultural Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) to analyze how actors plan opportunities for authenticity. CHAT describes generative interactions between participants as “co -configuration” (Engeström, 2004). The InsectLife project focuses on co- configuration between interacting activity systems as participants navigate contradictions that arise when they attempt to collaborate.

papers.authors: Pierre-Valery Njenji Tchetgen
papers.abstract: The Urban Griots Playground (UGP) study investigates how culturally grounded, embodied learning environments impact early literacy and socio- emotional development in young children through a family workshop series. Using the researcher -developed Drumball- Alphariddims system—a digital tool integrating rhythmic call- and-response—UGP helped scaffold literacy and social skills in five child -parent dyads over four weeks. Findings suggest that this embodied, rhythmic and multimodal approach stimulated  early literacy behaviors and social participation, though younger children struggled with the complexity of the Alphariddim code. The workshops also improved emotional understanding through storytelling and culturally relevant proverbs. While the study highlights the potential of culturally grounded, family-centered music-based interventions (MBI) for at-risk children, limitations such as small sample size and technological constraints call for further refinement and longitudinal research.

papers.title: Pursuits of Social Change: A Comparative Case Study of Youth Learning to Reduce Food Waste in School
papers.authors: Tesha Sengupta Irving, Hosun Kang, Nelly Tsai, Minjung Shin
papers.abstract: In the face of global polycrisis, we call for greater support for youth to learn about complex problems and make social change. In this comparative case analysis, we explore how high school students engaged in a socioeducational ecology designed for the study of food waste in a climate education class. Conceptually, we recontextualize an established framework in the Learning Sciences (Productive Disciplinary Engagement) to reframe engagement as pursuit - a collective, interest- driven traversal of settings and people over time (Jornet et al., 2025). papers.title: rin Jacob, Parastu Dubash, Mark Warschauer, Carolina Gimenez, Pamela Gonzalez, Hernan Gonzalez What Schooling is and What it Could Be: Exploring How We Learn the Discourses and Technologies of Public Education in School-Adjacent Spaces
papers.authors: Emma C. Gargroetzi, Karis Jones, Antero Garcia, Nicole Mirra, Jasmine Y. Ma, Christopher Ostrowdun, Lauren Vogelstein, Ali R. Blake, Carlos Nicolas Gómez Marchant, Alexandra R. Aguilar, Jyl Josephson, Nooreen Fatima
papers.abstract: In the US in recent years, public engagement in public schools has become highly politicized, reflecting the polarized discourses circulating in media and inflamed by national figures. “Official” spaces for public input exist alongside multiple less officially policy-relevant spaces where youth and adults learn and negotiate the function/ing of public education. This symposium examines how diverse school -adjacent spheres of publ ic life function as pedagogical spaces - spaces where the discourses and technologies of schooling are learned through the cognizant and non-cognizant design and organization of discourse and activity. The cases considered span from youth-centered spaces such as the school bus and a middle school debate team to a case examining the intersection of how news and social media is negotiated at a public committee meeting and closing with two contrasting examples of school district - sponsored public forums addressing issues such as overcrowding and budget. Symposium overview As persistent issues of inequality in educational spaces rise to the forefront of national conversations in the US, we are reminded that education and schooling is everyone’s business. Even those who are not presently children, parents, teachers, or school  administrators have at some point experienced school, learning through experience what school is, shaping ideas about what it should or could be, and licensing public commentary on education from people in all walks of life. Notably, the school building is not the only place where we learn what school is, what it can be, or how to participate in public discourse shaping policy in response to these questions. In this symposium we consider how people learn in and through school -adjacent spaces both what scho ol is or can be and how to participate in public discourse about school. In the US, public engagement in public schools (schools supported by public funds) has become a highly politicized space, reflecting the polarized and often vitriolic discourses circulating in media and inflamed by national figures. “Official” spaces for p ublic input, such as through the election of public school boards, open school board meetings, and district -sponsored public forums exist alongside multiple less officially policy - relevant spaces where youth and adults learn and negotiate the function/ing of public education, drawing on long histories and reflecting possibilities for our children’s futures. Public school boards, one type of semi-public forum for shaping public education, is one space where an official governing body has substantial power as it “(a) defines reality, (b) orders behavior, and (sometimes) (c) allocates resources accordingly” (Lev inson et al., 2009, p. 770). Public participation and commentary on policy making is one place we can look to to see how the status quo is maintained or challenged. On the one hand, public spaces like school boards can be places of possibility where citizens have the opportunity to affect policy making decisions, as described by Collins (2021): “This opportunity for efficacy [in affecting policy decisions] is particularly available at the local level, where schools boards and city councils govern within rea ch of the citizenry” ( p. 790). However, school board meetings in particular are often an authoritative and ritualistic (e.g., Robert’s rules of order) space where local politics and civic life collide in less-than-transformative ways. Learning to engage with the body politic of school boards, and likewise learning to participate in formal debate, requires learning genres of public comments, of argumentation, rebuttal, and the power of non -authorized policy actors (i.e., students, teachers, community members; Collins, 2021; Jenkins, 2022; Levinson et al., 2009; Tracy & Durfy, 2007). Other types of spaces organize public engagement with education in different ways, opening alternative affordances for learning and numerous ways that actors can be positioned. For instance, public engagement in participatory grassroots organizing efforts—building on affinity spaces as well as affordances of connected social media spaces—shows potential for citizenship that can organize into powerful vehicles for demanding critical and consequential change (Ito et al., 2015). This does not mean that informa l or grassroots organizers are inherently equitable, as social power differentials can lead to the privileging of certain narratives and inequitable results — particularly narratives driven by white supremacy (Ewing, 2018; Joffe-Walt et al., 2020). Youth participation in public narratives on education abound, but are seldom recognized as legitimate civic participation and may even be positioned as disrespectful or insubordinate (Kelly, 2020). Interactions in places such as social media or after -school clubs and activities provide insight into youth perspectives and the ways they both learn and teach the ways of talking, thinking, and participating in shaping the future of education and school. We are interested in how youth spaces such as the debate team or even school buses may be important political spheres for learning about schooling. Conceptual framework: School-adjacent spaces as pedagogical We examine how diverse school -adjacent spheres of public life function as pedagogical spaces - spaces where the discourses and technologies of schooling and public participation in public schooling are learned through the cognizant and non-cognizant design and organization of discourse and activity in those spaces. In other words, “space is treated as a product of social practice, not simply a frame for it” (Nespor, 2000, p.25). We bring together diverse cases in order to consider how different spaces beyond the school building may shape how the public learns what public school is or can be. We see this work as extending emerging work in the learning sciences that explores learning as political by examining learning in and as a feature of power in the political spheres of public life (Booker et al, 2014; Esmonde & Booker, 2016; The Politics Writing Collective, 2017). Moreover, we suggest that understanding these spaces as pedagogical  may provide critical insight into how our imaginations are shaped regarding what is possible in schools and add to work that “elucidate[s] the way that policy t ypically serves to reproduce existing structures of domination and inequality” (Levinson et al., 2009, p. 769) as well as looking at ways these policies can be disrupted. Format The cases considered span from youth-centered spaces such as the school bus and a middle school debate team to a case examining the intersection of how news and social media is negotiated at a public committee meeting and closing with two contrasting examp les of school district -sponsored public forums addressing issues such as overcrowding and budget. The symposium format intentionally brings together diverse cases in order to consider official and unofficial policy -relevant spaces, voices from youth and ad ults, and examples of both the perpetuation, disruption, and re -storying of existing narratives surrounding purposes and possibilities of public schooling. After each case, virtual and in-person participants will have time to discuss and compare the pedagogies of each case. The symposium itself will be briefly introduced by the Co -chairs, Karis Jones and Emma Gargroetzi. Each of the five cases will be presented. Following these presentations, Discussant Tanner Vea, with expansive expertise studying power, politics, and learni ng, particularly in social change efforts and design, will provide commentary on the necessity and potential of understanding school -adjacent spaces as pedagogically consequential for education and public school. A significant portion of the time will be h eld for discussion and conversation with attendees. We invite participants to consider with us: Where and how does learning across these five cases suggest reproduction or transformation in the face of material and discursive systems that shape schooling? How might unveiling these possibilities and constraints support new forms of learning and engagement with public education? Significance In a moment where high -stakes decisions about banning books, silencing history, restricting bathrooms access, and arming teachers with automatic weapons threaten the lives and livelihood of both children and adults in schools, the stakes of the political life of schools continue to grow. Yet, these decisions are largely made outside of schools themselves. This symposium contributes needed attention to the question of where and how people learn what can and should be expected from schools, and what it means to participate in conversations about these very topics. In framing and examining the activity of these school-adjacent spaces as pedagogical, we offer a lens that may be productive for uncovering insights about the design and organization of these spaces as products of social practice (Nespor, 2000). In unveiling the socially produced nature of these spaces, we leave them open for disruption, and can perhaps more freely imagine them being produced anew, with more just and joyful possibilities for the future. Re-storied journeys: The school bus and the narrative of public education Antero Garcia This paper explores the role of the school bus as a form of public discourse about education and the ways youth voices are largely silenced in their daily commutes as passengers to and from sites of formal education. Everyday, millions of students across the US rely on public school buses to get to and from school. These gigantic vehicles- brightly painted, hissing with hydraulic brake systems, and puttering away slightly below the speed limit improbably operate out of the vision of school policy and social discussion. These vehicles impact nearly every school in the US and yet seem to be invisible when it comes to discussions of schooling and structure. The fact that the school bus does not come up as a central policy discussion (except for when a global pan demic causes it to stop operation) is a reminder of how central the school bus is to the day-to-day operation of schooling. Despite not changing in design for nearly a century, the school bus’s function as an intervention on the educational outcomes of students in the US makes it the most substantial form of educational technology in this country (Garcia, in press). As a cognitive technology, the school bus disrupts education in two ways. First, its role in shifting school demographics post Brown v. Education  is so profound that the verb “busing” is synonymous with addressing desegregation mandates. Second, as a hulking piece o f machinery, the bus is a form of (albeit) archaic technology that acts on the lives of young people every day. Both of these disruptions are so persistent and long lasting that it’s arguable that they are even disruptions at this point rather than a part of the status quo. Spending a year of ethnographic participant -observation (Geertz, 1973) alongside young people on a school bus and engaging in historical research on the development of the school bus and the policies that structure it, this paper explores how public engagement with the sc hool bus reinforces an understanding of the bus as implicit and necessary in the operation of public schooling. Every moment of on -bus bullying, of traffic-control through the use of a blinking set of lights, and of picking up and dropping off of kids at l ocal stops is a reminder that these buses act as a part of the seamless infrastructure of American schooling (Edwards, 2021). Further, as a temporary space that reorients and transforms the behaviors and possibilities of its users, the archaic bus is also a reflection of contemporary representation of the role of platforms on education and policy (e.g. Gillespie, 2010; Srnicek, 2017). Finally, drawing on the work of Thomas and Stornaiuolo (2016), the narrative of the school bus is not fixed; we can “restory” it. While the narrative of the school bus conveys it as a sometimes uncomfortable but necessary component of how students interact with and participate in schooling in the US However, through shifting the gaze of schooling from a structural analysis of school systems to a humanistic perspective of young people’s learning opportunities, this paper argues that school buses might be sites for resistance, imagination, and realigning public discourse. Reconstructing debate as public pedagogy: Advocating for speculative civic futures Nicole Mirra Purpose This paper illuminates the organization of learning within a middle school debate team that sought to transform the activity of debate from an academic exercise to a critical enactment of public pedagogy aimed at envisioning new possibilities for civic life. Specifically, it examines how youth who identified as recently arrived immigrants remixed a policy debate topic asking them to consider “both sides” of immigration restrictions. papers.title: Cultivating Ensembles at ISLS
papers.authors: Marisa A. Holzapfel, Carolyn D. Sealfon, Barbara J. Natalizio, Raquell M. Holmes
papers.abstract: Large conference attendees often miss interesting sessions because of the conflicts of parallel programming. The authors, Cultivating Ensembles’ organizers, will model their innovative and intentional approach to this issue with the ISLS 2024 participants . We offer to lead a series of ongoing brief engagement activities throughout ISLS 2024 that allow participants to share their experiences from different sessions. We use a documented playful and inclusive approach to engage the broadest audience. Organizers The Cultivating Ensembles Organizing Committee (CE; formerly Cultivating Ensembles in STEM Education and Research) brings together people who create powerful learning environments through intentional collaboration across the arts, humanities, and sciences.  Activities include bi- annual conferences, community meetings, and coffee chats. CE creates a unique professional development environment where innovators learn from each other’s practice and discover and celebrate the interweaving of sciences, technologies, humanities, and the arts as human activities. People who collectively imagine, create, and explore our world are the heart of science, technology, engineering, mathematics, medicine, and the multitude of arts (Sealfon et al., 2023). Learn more about us at cultivatingensembles.org. Event description Organizers of Cultivating Ensembles (Holmes, 2022) welcome the Learning Sciences community in an interactive discovery of ensemble-building and its possibilities for research and education. We promote co-creative, inclusive environments where learning and growth occurs among individuals as a community, with collaborative, reflective inquiry and performance (Schon, 1983; Jaworski, 2006; Lobman, 2010; Holzman, 2016). At large conferences, participants sometimes suffer from the "Fear of Missing Out" (FOMO). To overcome this, we often have to accept the "Certainty of Missing Out" (COMO). To help  manage COMO, Cultivating Ensembles builds “share out” sessions into its conference schedules, where participants share what they learned in different parallel sessions, or even what they heard in the same session differently. These sessions use play and performance as collaborative exploration, an approach that views learning as a creative, social act (Knudsen and Shechtman, 2011; Martinez, 2011; Sawyer, R. K. 2004). In this workshop, we invite the Learning Sciences community to join us in a series of dynamic short co- generative sharing activities during the conference in which we will build an ensemble that explores through play the following questions (Sealfon et al., 2023; Hadzigeorgiou et al., 2012; Holzapfel et al., 2022): ● How does bringing our whole selves, inviting and valuing everyone’s contributions, impact how and what we learn? ● How do we build trust with the angst and discomfort that arise in interactive environments? ● How do we cultivate environments conducive to open, honest, and inclusive discussions? ● How can creativity influence science or optimize and innovate education and research? From the experience created together over our coffee chats, conferences (Martinez et al., 2023) and last year’s ISLS workshop (Sealfon et al., 2023), we invite the Learning Sciences community to collaborate to examine the following: ● How can we study the “intangible” values of conferences, communities, and co-creating something together? ● What does it mean to be participants in what we are studying? Can we study what we have not experienced? ● What does it mean to transform the metrics we use to be inclusive? We will facilitate daily activities throughout the conference. This friendly, interactive space will engage participants with each other about what they are learning and experiencing through the rest of the conference. We 67 off er an activity on each conference day that reflects the conference theme Learning as a cornerstone of healing, resilience, and community . We invite participants to approach the three sub- themes of healing, resilience, and community in creative, playful, and collaborative ways. Activities may include collective drawings, collages, games, structures, and bulletin boards. The final activity will include a synthesis and debrief of what we will have built together over the previous days. The result is a collaborative work of art that is unique and could only be created through the joint design of many different voices with different perspectives. Using this playful and creative approach, the conference and participants’ experiences can be reflected on more effectively. Expected outcomes for participants include: ● Experience and articulate the relationship of play and improvisation to cultivating an inclusive collective experience. ● Share and explore highlights of what each other is learning throughout the conference. ● Reflect on day -to-day interactions and how cultivating developmental ensembles impacts our teaching and research. ● Manifest understanding of new ideas through playful, embodied, and tangible experiences. ● Get to know other conference participants with similar interests and focuses. ● Gain a preliminary insight into the work of Cultivating Ensembles. Note that this is not a traditional workshop, but rather an experience that builds throughout the ISLS conference. By inviting participants to experience a new form of learning environment, we create the conditions for additional research questions, partnerships, and discoveries to emerge. We invite participants to continue building with us after the conference, for example through coffee chats hosted by Cultivating Ensembles throughout the year and the upcoming 2025 Cultivating Ensembles conference.
